claim_verdicts.evidence: git-merge, HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED: "Among the changes made to the common ancestor's version, non-overlapping ones (that is, you changed an area of the file while the other side left that area intact, or vice versa) are incorporated in the final result verbatim. When both sides made changes to the same area, however, Git cannot randomly pick one side over the other, and asks you to resolve it by leaving what both sides did to that area." Docs say "area" where the claim says "region (a run of neighbouring lines)"; same notion.

git-merge, "When it is not obvious how to reconcile the changes": "1. The HEAD pointer stays the same." … "4. For conflicting paths, the index file records up to three versions: stage 1 stores the version from the common ancestor, stage 2 from HEAD, and stage 3 from MERGE_HEAD … The working tree files contain the result of the merge operation; i.e. 3-way merge results with familiar conflict markers." … "6. No other changes are made." No commit is written and the branch tip is unchanged.
claim_verdicts.source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge — TRUE MERGE / HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-status, Short Format status-letter table: "U U  unmerged, both modified". Option -b/--branch: "Show the branch and tracking info even in short-format", and the output is preceded by a line "## <branchname> <tracking-info>". The captured run at stage-0 shows both forms: "UU total.sh" and "## conflict-demo".

git-merge: "The area where a pair of conflicting changes happened is marked with markers <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>. The part before the ======= is typically your side, and the part afterwards is typically their side." The diff3 example shows the order <<<<<<< yours:sample.txt / ||||||| base:sample.txt / ======= / >>>>>>> theirs:sample.txt, i.e. the ||||||| section sits directly above =======. Docs hedge with "typically" because rebase swaps the sides; for a merge the first section is the branch you are on.

git-merge: "By default, Git uses the same style as the one used by the 'merge' program from the RCS suite" and "The default format does not show what the original said in the conflicting area." — default writes two sides only. "An alternative style can be used by setting the merge.conflictStyle configuration variable to either diff3 or zdiff3"; both examples contain "||||||| base:sample.txt". So the claim as written holds, but diff3 is not the only style that writes the section (zdiff3 exists since Git 2.35, i.e. in pinned 2.46) — see issue on section 3.

git(1), -c <name>=<value>: "Pass a configuration parameter to the command. The value given will override values from configuration files. The <name> is expected in the same format as listed by git config (subkeys separated by dots)." It overrides config for that invocation only.

git-merge, HOW TO RESOLVE CONFLICTS: "Git will mark the conflicts in the working tree. Edit the files into shape and git add them to the index. Use git commit or git merge --continue to seal the deal." git-rebase: "For each file you edit, you need to tell Git that the conflict has been resolved. You can mark the conflict as resolved with git add <filename>." The negative half rests on absence: the documented flow describes no re-comparison of the staged text with either side; git merge --continue only "checks whether there is a (interrupted) merge in progress".
claim_verdicts.source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge — HOW TO RESOLVE CONFLICTS; https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase — DESCRIPTION

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-merge: "Edit the files into shape and git add them to the index. Use git commit or git merge --continue to seal the deal." git-rebase, MODE OPTIONS: "--continue  Restart the rebasing process after having resolved a merge conflict." and DESCRIPTION: "After resolving all of the conflicts, you can continue the rebasing process with git rebase --continue".

git-merge --abort: "Abort the current conflict resolution process, and try to reconstruct the pre-merge state." "If there were uncommitted worktree changes present when the merge started, git merge --abort will in some cases be unable to reconstruct these changes. It is therefore recommended to always commit or stash your changes before running git merge." git-rebase --abort: "Abort the rebase operation and reset HEAD to the original branch … Otherwise HEAD will be reset to where it was when the rebase operation was started."

git-rebase DESCRIPTION: "Replay the commits, one by one, in order." and "If there is a merge conflict during this process, git rebase will stop at the first problematic commit and leave conflict markers", after which --continue "Restart[s] the rebasing process" — so a stop is possible at each replayed commit. git-merge: "A merge stops if there's a conflict that cannot be resolved automatically or if --no-commit was provided" — one stop for the whole operation.

git-rebase, -m/--merge: "Note that a rebase merge works by replaying each commit from the working branch on top of the <upstream> branch. Because of this, when a merge conflict happens, the side reported as ours is the so-far rebased series, starting with <upstream>, and theirs is the working branch. In other words, the sides are swapped."

Read at the tag: scripts/git/conflict-demo.sh line 3 is "set -euo pipefail" and line 11 is "git -c merge.conflictStyle=diff3 merge --no-edit feature/currency || true". outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/conflict-demo.txt line 3 is "Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result." The lesson's wording "reports failure" is carried by that message; the exit-code inference is not made in the text and is not needed.

outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/conflict-demo.txt at the tag, lines 1-6: "Auto-merging total.sh" / "CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in total.sh" / "Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result." / blank / "what Git says about the working tree now:" / "UU total.sh". Matches the lesson's output block character for character.

Same captured file, lines 17-23: "<<<<<<< HEAD" / "echo $(( (total / 1000000) * 1000000 ))" / "||||||| 09c8526" / "echo \"$total\"" / "=======" / "echo \"$total đồng\"" / ">>>>>>> feature/currency". Lines 9-16 of the same listing carry the other eight lines of total.sh unfenced, so exactly one line conflicts.

git-playground/build-history.sh at stage-0 writes total.sh ending "echo \"$total\"", commits 'Add a second product', then runs "git branch feature/shipping" and "git branch feature/currency" BEFORE the sed that rewrites the echo on main; feature/currency's own sed then produces "echo \"$total đồng\"". The captured run labels the base section "||||||| 09c8526"; foundation.l2.git-merge-vs-rebase's ledger names the same commit as the merge base. I could not re-run git in this session to recompute the hash.

Captured file lines 25-35: after "abort puts everything back the way it was:" the next line is "## conflict-demo" (no path line), then total.sh printed with the last line "echo $(( (total / 1000000) * 1000000 ))" and no markers. The lesson replaces line 26 with "..." and says so in prose ("The ... marks one line cut from this listing"), which matches.

git-merge: "For conflicting paths, the index file records up to three versions: stage 1 stores the version from the common ancestor, stage 2 from HEAD, and stage 3 from MERGE_HEAD", and "git show :2:filename shows the HEAD version, and git show :3:filename shows the MERGE_HEAD version" — each stage is that branch's whole file, not the partially merged working-tree result. Taking one stage therefore discards the regions Git merged cleanly, e.g. main's comment line "# Round to millions so the invoice looks tidy." which feature/currency's total.sh does not have.
claim_verdicts.source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge — TRUE MERGE, HOW TO RESOLVE CONFLICTS

claim_verdicts.evidence: Labelled opinion and hedged in the lesson body ("usually touches more regions", "tends to follow"); it follows from claim 1 rather than from any documented rule. One restatement in section 8 drops the hedge — see the section 8 issue.

Value judgement about what a conflict means for a team; no documentation can settle it. The concrete part (both branches changed the last line deliberately) is already covered by claims 14-15. Wording drift in section 6 ("two correct pieces of work") is raised as an issue.

git-switch: "-c <new-branch>  Create a new branch named <new-branch> starting at <start-point> before switching to the branch"; "-q, --quiet  Quiet, suppress feedback messages"; "<start-point>  The starting point for the new branch." git-merge: "The --no-edit option can be used to accept the auto-generated message". Each option is documented as affecting branch creation, message output or the commit message only — nothing in how a conflict is detected or presented.

git-merge --abort: "Abort the current conflict resolution process, and try to reconstruct the pre-merge state" and "git merge --abort is equivalent to git reset --merge when MERGE_HEAD is present" — it acts on a merge that is in progress. Also: "A merge stops if there's a conflict that cannot be resolved automatically … At that point you can run git merge --abort or git merge --continue." Once the merge commit is written there is no MERGE_HEAD and no current conflict resolution process. I could not run git here to quote the refusal message.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the exclusivity "only when … merge.conflictStyle=diff3" is not in the ledger (claim 5 says only that diff3 writes the section and that the default writes two sides) and is false. git-merge: "An alternative style can be used by setting the merge.conflictStyle configuration variable to either diff3 or zdiff3"; the zdiff3 example also contains "||||||| base:sample.txt". A reader whose config is zdiff3 sees the shared version without the demo's -c flag, contradicting the lesson. Section 5's "without it Git writes only the two sides" has the same gap.
issues.fix: Section 3: replace "only when the command is run with `merge.conflictStyle=diff3`" with "only when the command is asked for it, as the demo script in section 5 does with `merge.conflictStyle=diff3`". Section 5: replace "without it Git writes only the two sides" with "with Git's default style only the two sides are written". Add the exclusivity-free wording to the ledger under claim 5.
issues.quote: written into a third section only when the command is run with `merge.conflictStyle=diff3`, as the demo script in section 5 does

issues.text: Over-generalisation: the bullet defines "unmerged" as a state and then attaches `UU` to it, as if UU were the unmerged code. git-status's Short Format lists seven unmerged pairs — DD, AU, UD, UA, DU, AA and UU — and UU specifically means "unmerged, both modified". Claim 3 is correctly narrower ("a path both sides modified"); the lesson text is not.
issues.fix: Change to: "unmerged — the state Git records for such a file; when both sides modified it, `git status --short` prints `UU` beside it, and no commit is written until you clear it."
issues.quote: unmerged — the state Git records for such a file; `git status --short` prints `UU` beside it

issues.text: "all it did was" understates what a stopped merge has already done. git-merge: "Paths that merged cleanly are updated both in the index file and in your working tree." The lesson itself relies on this in section 6 ("everywhere else the file on disk already holds the right answer") and in quiz q5 option b, so the two statements disagree.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "it wrote both versions between markers, marked the file unmerged, and put everything it could merge into the file and the staging area — leaving your history untouched."
issues.quote: all it did was write both versions between markers and mark the file unmerged, leaving your history untouched

issues.text: The branch-age heuristic is stated flatly here, while claim 18 records it as "A tendency, not a rule: a long-lived branch touching files nobody else touched conflicts nowhere" and sections 5 and 9 hedge it ("usually", "tends to"). A Connections line that drops the hedge reads as a law.
issues.fix: Match the hedged form: "… a branch that lands in a day usually changes few regions, while one left alone for weeks usually changes many and so has more places to collide."
issues.quote: a branch that lands in a day changes few regions, while one left alone for weeks changes many and has more places to collide

issues.text: "two correct pieces of work" asserts more than claim 19, which says a conflict is what "two deliberate changes to the same lines look like". A conflict says nothing about either change being correct — one side may well be wrong; Git only reports that both touched the same region.
issues.fix: Replace "two correct pieces of work touched the same lines" with "two deliberate changes touched the same lines", keeping the rest of the bullet unchanged.
issues.quote: Actually it means two correct pieces of work touched the same lines

issues.text: Unlisted claim: "running it twice changes nothing" is not in the ledger and is only approximately true — scripts/up.sh at stage-0 runs `docker compose up -d --build --wait`, which rebuilds images and recreates containers whenever their inputs changed. The same sentence was already flagged in foundation.l2.git-merge-vs-rebase's technical review and was copied here unchanged.
issues.fix: Change the parenthesis to "(it prepares the example system; it is safe to run again)", or drop it and keep only "run `scripts/up.sh`".
issues.quote: run `scripts/up.sh` (it prepares the example system; running it twice changes nothing)

issues.text: Unlisted claim in the prerequisite recap: "the newest commit the two sides share" assumes a single merge base. The prerequisite lesson's ledger states it with the caveat "a tangled history can have more than one; here there is exactly one"; this recap presents the singular as always true.
issues.fix: Write "both commands start from a commit the two sides share — here the newest one", or add the recap sentence to this lesson's ledger citing the prerequisite's claim 1.
issues.quote: both commands start from the newest commit the two sides share
